analysis.one_liner: Requires drug makers to honor 340B discounts no matter how safety-net clinics dispense the drugs.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in July 2025 with two cosponsors and referred to the Senate health committee, where it has not moved.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the 340B program, safety-net hospitals and clinics buy outpatient drugs at steep discounts, and many of them dispense those drugs through outside 'contract pharmacies.' In recent years some drug manufacturers have refused to ship discounted drugs to those pharmacies or imposed conditions on the discounts. This bill writes into law that manufacturers must honor the discounts no matter where or how the drug is dispensed, bans those restrictions, and lets the government fine violators up to $2 million per day [S2].
analysis.who_benefits: Patients of community health centers, rural hospitals, and other safety-net providers who rely on contract pharmacies to fill prescriptions, especially for expensive specialty drugs. The clinics and hospitals themselves also gain purchasing power.

how_it_helps.text: The bill requires manufacturers to offer 340B discounted prices on drugs bought by covered entities 'regardless of the manner or location in which the drug is dispensed,' covering contract pharmacies [S2].

It bars manufacturers from placing conditions on discounted purchases, including limiting delivery, purchase mechanisms, or dispensing locations, or singling out covered entities with restrictions [S2].

It adds civil monetary penalties of up to $2,000,000 for each day a manufacturer intentionally violates the new requirements, and requires the Secretary to set up a process for covered entities to file violation claims [S2].

The bill's findings note the 340B inflation penalty saved $7 billion in Medicare Part D spending from 2013 to 2017, and that contract pharmacy arrangements are often the only way safety-net entities can access specialty drugs like cancer treatments [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Pharmaceutical manufacturers, who would lose the ability to restrict how discounted 340B drugs are dispensed and could face daily fines. Some of that cost could surface as higher list prices, which hit insurers and patients indirectly.

drawbacks.text: Manufacturers and some policy analysts argue that a growing share of 340B discounts flows to large hospital systems and for-profit pharmacy chains without lowering prices for uninsured or underinsured patients, and that this bill locks in that flow rather than requiring savings to reach patients directly [S2].

By making the contract pharmacy channel mandatory, the bill entrenches the middlemen — including national retail chains — between the discount and the patient, and it does not require covered entities to report what they do with the savings [S2].
Daily fines up to $2 million and a ban on most manufacturer conditions could push manufacturers to raise list prices to offset the deeper effective discounts, raising costs for everyone else [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For patients who depend on safety-net clinics and contract pharmacies for specialty drugs, the bill protects real access that manufacturers have been restricting. The honest cost is that it strengthens a discount program whose savings often enrich hospital systems and pharmacy chains rather than patients directly, and manufacturers may recover the lost margin through higher list prices elsewhere.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which has taken no action on it [S4].

narrative.text: Sen. Peter Welch introduced the bill on July 22, 2025, with Sen. Jeff Merkley as its other cosponsor; it was read twice and referred to the HELP Committee [S4].
The bill has two cosponsors, both Senate Democrats [S3].
No hearings, markups, or votes on the bill appear in its action history since referral [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers are better off so far, because the restrictions this bill would ban remain in place while it sits without committee action.

for.name: Sen. Peter Welch
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the HELP Committee [S4].

sides.party_line_note: Both sponsors and both cosponsors are Senate Democrats, but no committee or floor votes have occurred, so no partisan split can be measured [S3].

industries.note: They would have to honor 340B discounts through any dispensing channel and could face fines up to $2 million per day. Their interest in keeping restrictions runs against the access the bill protects for safety-net patients [S2].

industries.industry: Contract pharmacy chains and specialty pharmacies
industries.note: The bill locks in outside pharmacies as the dispensing channel for 340B drugs, securing their role and margins. Some are for-profit chains whose share of the discount does not necessarily reach patients [S2].

industries.industry: Safety-net hospitals, clinics, and health centers
industries.note: Covered entities regain unrestricted access to discounted drugs, which the bill says lets them stretch resources to serve more patients [S2].

analysis.trajectory: With only two cosponsors, no committee action in months, and a committee controlled by leadership scheduling priorities, the bill is likely to sit in committee unless it gains substantially more support; most referred bills without early committee action never reach a vote.
